claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloys have dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries.
Internal colony boundaries are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile loading.
A controlled post-solidification annealing treatment can induce nanoscale secondary-phase precipitation.
The annealing treatment can localize the nanoscale precipitates selectively at lamellar colony internal boundaries.
An appropriate annealing temperature-time window can produce nanoscale precipitation without coarsening the primary lamellar phases.
An appropriate annealing temperature-time window can avoid embrittlement while maintaining similar overall phase fractions.
Boundary-localized nanoscale precipitates enhance interfacial cohesion.
The nanoscale precipitates pin the internal colony boundaries.
Boundary-localized precipitates reduce effective stress concentrations and blunt crack tips.
Local interfacial reinforcement by the precipitates increases yield strength.
Limiting microcrack initiation and propagation delays catastrophic failure and increases room-temperature tensile ductility.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the heat-treated alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the heat-treated alloy will have higher ultimate tensile strength.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the heat-treated alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile ductility.
The intervention is expected to work only for eutectic high-entropy alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures.
The intervention is effective only within an annealing window that avoids lamellar coarsening and secondary-phase embrittlement.
Overly coarse or continuous interfacial phases could embrittle the alloy.
